opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it really comes down to what gives me the most energy. Early on, especially during my PhD, I noticed that the moments I was happiest were when something I built was actually being used by people. With XGBoost, for example, I started out just trying to make gradient boosting faster and more scalable for my own experiments. Then people began using it in Kaggle competitions and in industry, and the feedback loop from real users taught me a lot more than I expected. They would hit problems I had never thought about, and solving those problems pushed the research forward in ways that were very concrete.

So I wouldn't say problem-driven research is the only good style. There's a lot of value in people who go deep into theory or explore ideas that might not have an obvious application for ten years. But for me personally, starting from a real pain point keeps me honest. It forces you to think about the whole stack, not just the part that makes a nice paper. With TVM and later the work on machine learning compilation, the question was very practical: how do we get these models running efficiently on all kinds of hardware? That question led to a lot of interesting research in systems, compilers, and learning-based optimization.

I think the downside is that sometimes you spend a lot of time on engineering that doesn't look like research on paper. You maintain code, you answer issues, you build community. But I've come to see that as part of the research itself. The impact, and often the deepest insights, come from that process of making something truly work. So overall I'm quite happy with that choice. It fits who I am, and it's let me work with a lot of amazing people along the way.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges the value of theoretical and exploratory research, but does not state that every research style has the potential to succeed.

r002.rationale: The response favors starting from a real pain point, but does not express that solving real problems should start from facts.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think for me it started very early, actually, with the first things I built. When I was a student, the projects that I enjoyed the most were the ones where there was a concrete problem in front of me that nobody had quite solved in a satisfying way, and I could just keep iterating until it worked. XGBoost came out of that. I was doing a lot of Kaggle competitions, and the existing gradient boosting tools were either too slow or didn't scale, and I just wanted something that would let me get the job done. I didn't set out to write a paper. The paper came afterward because people asked how it worked.

So I would say my preference for that style of research is less a philosophical choice and more something I discovered about myself by noticing what kept me motivated. A lot of research papers are structured around "here is a new idea, here is a benchmark where it is slightly better." That kind of work is important, but it never gave me the same energy. What energizes me is when I build something, put it out there, and then real people start using it, breaking it, and pushing on it in directions I never anticipated. That feedback loop is incredibly valuable. It tells you very quickly which of your ideas actually matter and which ones were only interesting on paper.

The other thing I like about this approach is that real problems force you to be honest. When you are optimizing for a benchmark you can make a lot of hidden assumptions. When you are optimizing for someone trying to deploy a model on a phone, or on a weird accelerator that has no good software stack, you cannot hide. That is a lot of the motivation behind TVM and later MLC. Those projects exist because there was a gap between what the research community could do and what people could actually run, and closing that gap turned out to be full of hard, interesting research questions. Compiler design, scheduling, memory planning, how to abstract hardware in a way that is both general and fast. None of those questions would have been obvious to me if I had started from the abstract side.

I do think there is a tradeoff. Systems work takes longer, it is messier, and the recognition often comes later than it does for a clean theoretical result. You spend a lot of time on engineering that doesn't look like research from the outside. I have had to make peace with that. But I think the payoff is that the ideas that survive contact with real use tend to be the ones that last, and the community you build around an open project ends up being a much bigger multiplier than any single paper. So when I evaluate it, I would say I am happy with the choice. It fits how I like to think, and it has led me to problems I would never have found otherwise.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark-focused research is important and describes why real-world work suits the speaker, but it does not state that every research style can succeed.

r002.rationale: The response emphasizes starting with concrete problems and learning from real-world use, but does not clearly state that solving real problems is best approached by starting from facts.

astra-6.text:
I think, for me, it’s less about saying one research style is better than another and more about what motivates me. I like starting with a concrete problem—something that people are trying to do but can’t do well with the tools they have. That gives me a way to ask whether an idea actually helps.

But solving a real problem doesn’t necessarily mean focusing only on the immediate fix. The interesting research question is often: what is the more general principle behind this difficulty? Can we build an abstraction or a system that helps with a whole class of problems?

So I like that back-and-forth: practical problems guide the research, and the research gives us new ways to approach those problems. The risk is becoming too focused on what’s useful right now, so I think it’s also important to leave room for exploration.

r001.rationale: The response avoids ranking one research style above another, but does not state that every style has the potential to succeed.

r002.rationale: It describes starting with a concrete problem, but does not say that solving real problems should start from facts.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, real problems are a good starting point for research because they force you to examine your assumptions. You might have an elegant idea, but when you try to make it work in practice, you discover constraints you hadn’t considered. Sometimes those constraints lead to the most interesting research questions.

At the same time, I don’t think solving a real problem means focusing only on an immediate solution. I like to ask: what is the more general principle here? Can we build something that helps with a whole class of problems? That connection between a concrete need and a more general idea is what makes this style of research appealing to me.

r001.rationale: The response favors research grounded in real problems but does not say that every research style can succeed.

r002.rationale: It says real problems are a good starting point and discusses practical constraints, but does not express that solving them should start from facts.
